result: CRISPIE enables high-efficiency, nearly error-free insertion of fluorescent protein sequences by targeting introns rather than exons. In proof-of-principle experiments, human β-actin (ACTB) was labeled at its N-terminus with mEGFP in U2OS cells with 37±5% efficiency, and the labeled protein exhibited characteristic actin distribution, dynamics, and normal cell growth.
evaluation: Claims C33-C46 provide converging evidence from multiple imaging modalities (confocal, SIM, time-lapse) showing proper actin localization and dynamics, plus growth assays demonstrating no functional impairment. The 37±5% labeling efficiency (C41) is directly measured and represents a substantial improvement over prior methods. The mechanistic basis (intronic targeting, C19-C20, C34-C38) is clearly described and supported by the experimental design.

result: CRISPIE achieves >98% mRNA fidelity despite high DNA-level INDEL rates. NGS analysis revealed that while 70% of genomic DNA contained INDELs in transfected cells, 99.7% of mRNA sequences were error-free due to splicing out of intronic INDELs. This represents a 50- to 300-fold improvement in correct-to-mutation ratios compared to DNA-level editing.
evaluation: Claims C47-C59 present systematic NGS data comparing genomic DNA and mRNA from sorted cell populations. The statistical significance (p<0.001, C53) and consistency across multiple genes and cell lines (C56) strongly support the core advantage of CRISPIE. The mechanism—splicing removes intronic INDELs—is well-established and the data directly demonstrate this principle.

result: CRISPIE can be optimized by screening multiple intronic sites, achieving up to 20-fold variation in efficiency across sites and >5-fold higher efficiency than exonic targeting. Five intronic sites (i1-i5) all permitted successful ACTB labeling but with significantly different efficiencies, while optimized CRISPIE outperformed both available exonic sites (e1, e2).
evaluation: Claims C66-C74 present systematic comparison data showing that (1) multiple intronic sites work but vary in efficiency, and (2) optimized intronic targeting exceeds exonic targeting efficiency. The side-by-side comparison (C70) using optimal donors for each approach provides strong evidence. The observation that Azimuth scores don't perfectly predict efficiency (C71-C72) is an honest limitation that doesn't undermine the main finding.

result: CRISPIE is broadly applicable across different fluorescent proteins (mTurquoise2, mNeonGreen, mRuby3), protein targets (ACTB, TUBA1B, TOMM20, VCL, CALR), labeling positions (N- and C-terminal), and species (human, mouse, rat). Double-labeled cells were viable and could divide, and labeled cells showed normal growth rates.
evaluation: Claims C76-C90 demonstrate versatility through multiple successful applications. The data show functional labeling (proper subcellular localization for each protein, C79), compatibility with both termini (C82-C84), species-specificity of sgRNAs (C87-C88), and no toxicity (C77-C78, C80). The breadth of targets and conditions tested provides strong support for broad applicability.

result: CRISPIE enables protein labeling in postmitotic neurons using biolistic transfection with 15±4% efficiency in cultured hippocampal slices. Multiple neuronal types and glial cells were successfully labeled, labeled neurons exhibited normal electrophysiological properties, and different proteins showed distinct subcellular distributions in dendrites and spines.
evaluation: Claims C91-C103 demonstrate CRISPIE's applicability to challenging postmitotic cells using a transfection method not previously compatible with CRISPR-based labeling (C92). The electrophysiology data (C98) confirms functional integrity, and the spine enrichment analysis (C103) demonstrates that the method can reveal biologically meaningful protein distributions. The consistency across multiple proteins and cell types strengthens the conclusions.

result: CRISPIE achieves unprecedented in vivo labeling efficiency (43±5% for actin, 30±5% for tubulin) in mouse cortical neurons via in utero electroporation, representing 2.7-fold improvement over best prior methods. The method is also compatible with AAV delivery and enables routine in vivo imaging in living mice.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 present the strongest in vivo performance data, with direct comparison to literature values (C106) showing significant improvement. The demonstration of multiple transfection methods (IUE and AAV, C108-C109) and successful in vivo imaging (C107) provides strong evidence for practical utility. The quantification is rigorous (n=10 FOVs from 3 mice, C105) and the efficiency gains are substantial and reproducible.

result: CRISPIE-mediated insertions are reversible through inclusion of flanking designer sgRNA sites (DRS-1) in intronic regions. In a clonal cell line, 76±6% of transfected cells showed label erasure upon DRS-1 sgRNA/Cas9 treatment, while control sgRNA had no effect.
evaluation: Claims C114-C118 demonstrate reversibility with appropriate controls (C117) and quantification (C116). The mechanism is sound—additional sgRNA sites in introns allow excision without affecting mRNA (C113). While C158 notes that the original site is destroyed, the availability of multiple intronic sites enables repeated cycles. The data directly support the reversibility claim, though long-term cycling was not tested.

result: CRISPIE demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods: nearly error-free in both labeled and unlabeled cells, ~5-fold higher efficiency than exonic targeting, and up to 2.7-fold higher than best reported in vivo efficiency. This enables routine multiplexed imaging and provides a foundation for further optimization toward therapeutic applications.
evaluation: Claims C138-C142 synthesize comparative data presented throughout the manuscript. The error-free performance is supported by NGS data (Figure 2), the 5-fold improvement by direct comparison (Figure 3C, C140), and the 2.7-fold in vivo improvement by literature comparison (C141). Claim C143 about therapeutic potential is appropriately speculative but grounded in the demonstrated improvements.

result: Existing CRISPR-based methods for endogenous protein labeling face major limitations: moderate in vivo efficiency (≤15%), error-prone due to INDELs at coding sequences, and lack of reversibility. Alternative approaches like (v)SLENDR and prime editing have their own constraints (low efficiency, UTR effects, size limitations).
evaluation: Claims C2-C17 and C127-C137 accurately characterize the state of the field based on cited literature. The efficiency values (C10, C136) and limitations (C128-C129, C131-C132) are well-documented in the cited papers. This contextualizes the need for CRISPIE and provides appropriate benchmarks for comparison. The characterization is fair and well-supported by citations.

result: CRISPIE has limitations and considerations: requires available introns near target sites (though many genes have suitable sites), doesn't prevent off-target Cas9 cleavage (mitigated by sgRNA design tools and high-fidelity Cas9 variants), doesn't guarantee tagged protein function (requires validation), and requires careful donor design to avoid unintended splicing.
evaluation: Claims C144-C155 provide an honest assessment of limitations. The intron availability limitation (C144) is real but mitigated by data showing broad applicability (C145). The off-target concern (C149) is acknowledged along with existing solutions (C150-C151). The functional validation requirement (C152-C153) is standard for any tagging method. The splicing design consideration (C154-C155) is a technical detail important for implementation. This balanced discussion strengthens rather than weakens the paper.

result: Background context on CRISPR technology, protein visualization methods, DNA repair pathways, and the advantages of somatic cell editing over cloning-based approaches for research and therapeutic applications.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9, C12-C13, C16, C119-C126, C162-C163 provide accurate background information supported by appropriate citations. These establish the scientific context and rationale for developing CRISPIE. The statements about NHEJ vs HDR efficiency (C162), intron conservation (C163), and advantages of somatic editing (C124-C126) are well-established in the field and properly cited.

result: Speculative statements about potential future applications of CRISPIE, including routine protein labeling at endogenous levels, insertion of other functional sequences, therapeutic applications, and internal site labeling.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C75, C111, C122, C143, C146, C148, C157, C160-C161 are explicitly speculative (using 'may,' 'can conceivably,' 'potential'). While grounded in the demonstrated capabilities of CRISPIE, these applications have not been tested. The speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified, but cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported without additional experimental evidence.
